readerTitle: Why the Ritz-Carlton lets staff spend $2,000 without asking
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Ritz-Carlton의 직원 재량권) + 실제 연구·논문 (Oncken & Wass, 1974) + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 회사 고객지원팀, 청소 서비스 업체)
insight: 위임은 일을 넘기는 것이 아니라 결정을 넘기는 것이다. 대화가 끝난 뒤 '다음 수'를 누가 쥐고 있는지가 위임의 성패를 가른다.
misconception: 위임은 할 일을 나눠 주는 것이고, 중요한 결정은 여전히 관리자가 내려야 안전하다.

sources.text: Oncken, W. Jr. & Wass, D. L. (1974). Management Time: Who's Got the Monkey? Harvard Business Review, Nov–Dec 1974.
The Ritz-Carlton Leadership Center, materials on employee empowerment (the $2,000 guideline)
고객지원팀, 청소 업체 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Ritz-Carlton의 '직원 1인이 고객 문제 해결에 최대 $2,000까지 승인 없이 사용' 규칙은 Ritz-Carlton Leadership Center 자료와 여러 언론에서 반복 인용됩니다. 기준이 '고객당', '건당', '하루당' 중 무엇인지 자료마다 다르므로 카드에는 'to make things right for a guest'로만 적었습니다. 현재도 유지되는 정책인지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
Oncken & Wass의 '원숭이(monkey)' 비유와 'Let me think about it'으로 원숭이가 관리자 등에 올라탄다는 설명은 HBR 1974년 원문 내용입니다. 카드 문장은 원문을 직접 인용하지 않고 요약했습니다. 원문 표현과 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.
위임 권한의 단계(알아보고 보고 → 추천 → 결정 후 보고 → 알아서 결정)는 Oncken & Wass 및 여러 관리 문헌에 나오는 일반적 구분을 단순화한 것입니다. 특정 프레임워크 이름은 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the Ritz-Carlton lets staff spend $2,000 without asking
body: At Ritz-Carlton hotels, staff have long been allowed to spend up to $2,000 to make things right for a guest. No manager's approval needed.
In many companies, a team member can't approve a $50 refund. The difference isn't just trust. It's what the manager hands over.

image.label: Hotel housekeeper handing a guest a small gift at the door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 호텔 복도에서 객실 청소 직원이 투숙객에게 작은 선물 상자를 건네는 장면. 뒤편 멀리 매니저 책상은 비어 있음. 실제 호텔 로고·유니폼 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: An agent asks you about a refund.
body: You lead a customer support team at a software company. An experienced agent stops by: an angry user wants a refund for a month the app was down for them. You're between meetings.

options.text: "Leave it with me. I'll look into it and get back to you."
options.feedback: It feels helpful and safe. But the next step is now yours, the customer waits on your calendar, and the agent learns to bring you the next one too.

options.text: "Give them one month's refund and a polite apology."
options.feedback: Fast, and the customer is helped today. But you made the decision, so next time the agent will ask again.

options.text: "What do you suggest? Refunds up to one month are your call. Tell me what you did on Friday."
options.feedback: The agent leaves holding the decision, with a clear limit and a check-in. You give up a little control and gain time, speed and a stronger agent.

cards.title: Not a task. A problem to own.
body: The $2,000 limit isn't an invitation to spend. It tells staff two things: the guest's problem is **theirs to solve**, and how far they can go.
The person who hears the complaint is usually the one who can fix it fastest. If they must find a manager first, the guest waits and the moment is lost.

image.label: Two paths: complaint to manager and back, versus complaint fixed on the spot
image.brief: 두 갈래 흐름도. 위쪽: 손님 불만 → 직원 → 매니저 찾기 → 승인 → 해결 (시계 아이콘 여러 개). 아래쪽: 손님 불만 → 직원이 바로 해결 (시계 하나). 아래쪽을 밝은 색으로 강조.

cards.title: Delegating
body: **Delegating** means handing someone an outcome and the authority to make the decisions it needs, within clear limits.

Handing out tasks is different. "Call the customer" is a task. "Make this customer happy, up to one month's refund" is delegation. The first keeps every decision with you. The second moves the decisions to the person doing the work.

cards.title: Who's got the monkey?
body: In a classic 1974 Harvard Business Review article, William Oncken Jr. and Donald Wass called each problem a *monkey*. When an employee brings one and the manager says "Let me think about it," the monkey jumps onto the manager's back.
Do that all day and the manager falls behind while the team waits. Their fix: the monkey leaves with the person who brought it, with an agreed next step and a time to check in.

image.label: A small monkey hopping from an employee's shoulder to a manager's
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 직원 어깨 위 작은 원숭이가 "Let me think about it"이라는 말풍선과 함께 매니저 어깨로 뛰어오르는 장면. 매니저 책상에는 이미 원숭이 여러 마리. 귀엽고 가벼운 톤.

cards.eyebrow: How far to hand it over
cards.title: Delegation comes in levels.
body: You don't have to hand over everything at once. Pick a level for each decision:
list: **Decide** on your own, no report needed
cards.callout: Choose by risk and experience. Then move people up a level as they prove it.

cards.title: Handing over isn't walking away.
body: You still own the result. Delegating to someone without the skill or the context sets them up to fail. That's abandoning them, not empowering them.
Check-ins aren't micromanaging if you agree on them up front. And don't delegate only the dull work. People notice when the interesting decisions never leave your desk.

cards.title: Now it's a cleaning business.
body: You run a home cleaning company. Your new crew lead calls you from every job: a client wants the balcony done too, another wants a different time next week. You spend your day on the phone.

options.text: Keep taking the calls. Clients are too important to risk
options.feedback: Every client decision stays safe with you, but you become the bottleneck and the lead never learns to judge.

options.text: Tell the lead to handle everything and stop calling
options.feedback: The phone goes quiet, but with no limits the lead must guess. One big mistake and you'll likely take it all back.

options.text: Add-ons under an hour and schedule changes are theirs. Bigger asks: call with a suggestion. Review the log weekly
options.feedback: Small decisions move to the person on site, big ones still reach you with a recommendation. You trade a little control for your time and a lead who grows.

cards.title: Delegate decisions, not just tasks.
body: Hand over the outcome, the authority and the limits. Then make sure the next move leaves the room with the other person.
**Try it today:** next time someone brings you a problem, ask "What do you suggest?" and agree who does what by when.
